title: Aseptic technique and invasive devices
blurb: Protect Key-Parts and Key-Sites with aseptic non-touch technique, and care for cannulas and urinary catheters to prevent infection.
question: A nursing associate is preparing an IV antibiotic to give through a peripheral cannula using aseptic non-touch technique. Which part of the equipment is a Key-Part that must not be touched?

teach.h: Asepsis means protecting the critical parts
teach.body: Aseptic technique prevents harmful organisms being introduced from hands, equipment or the environment into a patient. Aseptic Non Touch Technique (ANTT) is the widely used UK framework. Its core idea is Key-Part and Key-Site protection: identify the parts that, if contaminated, are most likely to cause infection, and make sure they only touch other aseptic Key-Parts or Key-Sites. In plain words: work out what must stay clean, then never let your fingers or the environment touch it.
teach.cite: ANTT Clinical Practice Framework (The-ASAP); NICE CG139 1.4

rows.label: Examples
values: Syringe tip, needle, needle-free connector, catheter tip
Cannula insertion site, surgical wound, urethral meatus at insertion

teach.caption: Inactive Key-Parts such as closed IV ports cannot be kept aseptic between uses, so they are cleaned before use.

values: Short (about 20 minutes or less), few small Key-Parts
Longer, complex, many or large Key-Parts

Urinary catheter insertion; central line insertion

teach.caption: If during Standard-ANTT a Key-Part or Key-Site must be touched directly, change to sterile gloves.

teach.h: Giving an IV drug with Standard-ANTT
items: Clean the tray (general aseptic field) and let it dry; hand hygiene.
Prepare the drug without touching Key-Parts; keep the syringe tip capped.
At the bedside, hand hygiene and non-sterile gloves.
Clean the needle-free connector or port with chlorhexidine in 70% alcohol and let it dry.
Flush with sterile 0.9% sodium chloride to check patency, give the drug, flush again.
Clean the port after access, dispose of waste, remove gloves, hand hygiene, record.

Recommendation
rows: Before inserting a cannula or PICC
Chlorhexidine gluconate in 70% alcohol, allowed to dry
Only if sweating or oozing; replace with transparent dressing ASAP
Leave for the life of the cannula if intact
Change every 7 days, or sooner if loose or moist
Clean with chlorhexidine in 70% alcohol before and after access

teach.h: Urinary catheter: from decision to removal

steps.label: Aseptic insertion
steps.sub: sterile gloves; 10 mL sterile water in adult balloon

steps.label: Closed system
steps.sub: do not break the connection without reason

steps.label: Daily care
steps.sub: meatus washed with soap and water

teach.caption: NICE CG139: 10 mL sterile water for the balloon in adults, 3-5 mL in children.

teach.body: Decontaminate your hands and wear new non-sterile gloves before handling the catheter or bag. Keep the bag below bladder level and off the floor, use a link bag overnight so the system stays closed, and empty it often enough to keep urine flowing and prevent reflux. Take urine specimens from the sampling port using an aseptic technique. Bladder washouts or instillations must not be used to prevent infection. Change catheters only when clinically necessary or per the manufacturer.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Nurse Joy and Mr Bernard
teach.body: Mr Bernard, 79, has an indwelling catheter. Joy finds his drainage bag on the floor and later hooked above the bed rail. She repositions it below his bladder on a stand, explaining that a bag above the bladder allows urine to flow back. His daughter asks for weekly washouts 'to stop infections'. Joy explains that NICE advises against washouts for this purpose, supports daily meatal washing and good fluid intake, and asks the team to review whether he still needs the catheter.

teach.text: 'Non-sterile gloves' does not mean 'non-aseptic'. In Standard-ANTT the asepsis comes from never touching Key-Parts and Key-Sites, not from the gloves. If you will need to touch a Key-Part or Key-Site directly, that is the moment to switch to sterile gloves.

items: ANTT protects Key-Parts (critical equipment parts) and Key-Sites (wounds, device sites) by non-touch technique.
Standard-ANTT: short, simple, general aseptic field, usually non-sterile gloves. Surgical-ANTT: complex, critical aseptic field, sterile gloves.
Cannula: chlorhexidine in 70% alcohol, transparent dressing, clean hubs before and after access, flush with 0.9% sodium chloride.
Catheter: aseptic insertion, closed system, bag below bladder and off the floor, sample from the port, no washouts to prevent infection.
Review the need for any device and remove it as soon as possible.

summary: You can now identify Key-Parts and Key-Sites, choose Standard or Surgical-ANTT and apply NICE CG139 to cannula and catheter care. You can also explain why devices should be reviewed and removed as soon as they are no longer needed.

A.q: Tom is preparing an intravenous antibiotic to give through Mrs Lewis's peripheral cannula using ANTT. Which is a Key-Part?
options: The outside of the syringe barrel she holds
The plunger of the syringe
The syringe tip that connects to the hub
The label on the antibiotic vial
A.why: Key-Parts are the critical parts of equipment that touch Key-Sites, the infusion or other active Key-Parts; the syringe tip connects to the cannula hub.

whyNot.0: The barrel is handled during the procedure and does not enter the patient's circulation.
whyNot.1: The plunger is pushed by hand and is not a route into the patient.
whyNot.3: The vial label does not contact the drug pathway or the patient.

A.q: Before inserting a peripheral cannula into the forearm of Mr Malik, 45, how should the nurse decontaminate the skin?
options: With chlorhexidine gluconate in 70% alcohol, then let it dry
With soap and water, then dry with a paper towel
With 70% alcohol on its own, then insert the cannula straight away
With povidone-iodine, then wipe it off with sterile saline
A.why: NICE CG139 recommends chlorhexidine gluconate in 70% alcohol before inserting a peripheral vascular access device or PICC. Letting it dry completes its action.

whyNot.1: Soap and water cleans visible dirt but is not the recommended antiseptic before cannulation.
whyNot.2: Alcohol alone is not the recommended agent, and inserting before it dries reduces its effect.
whyNot.3: CG139 recommends chlorhexidine in 70% alcohol, and antiseptic is not wiped off before insertion.

A.q: Mr Patel's urinary drainage bag has been placed on the floor. Where should it be positioned?
options: Above the bladder to aid drainage
Below the bladder and off the floor
Level with the bladder, on the bed beside him
On the floor beside the bed frame
A.why: NICE CG139 1.2.5.6: drainage bags should be below the level of the bladder and should not be in contact with the floor.

whyNot.0: A bag above the bladder allows urine to flow back towards it, increasing infection risk.
whyNot.2: Level with the bladder does not allow free drainage and can cause reflux.
whyNot.3: Contact with the floor contaminates the bag and outlet.

B.q: Nadia is redressing a deep sacral cavity wound using Standard-ANTT with non-sterile gloves. She realises she will need to touch the wound bed directly to pack it. What should she do?
options: Continue with non-sterile gloves, taking care
Use sterile forceps for all of the packing from now on
Change to sterile gloves before touching the Key-Site
Wash the gloves with handrub, then touch the wound
B.why: If a Key-Part or Key-Site must be touched directly during Standard-ANTT, sterile gloves are introduced to reduce the risk of touch contamination (ANTT framework).

whyNot.0: Non-sterile gloves are acceptable only when Key-Sites are not touched.
whyNot.1: Forceps can help, but she has identified that direct touch is needed; that requires sterile gloves.
whyNot.3: Gloves must never be decontaminated with handrub; it does not make them sterile.

B.q: After inserting a peripheral cannula into the hand of Mrs Agnes, 88, the nurse needs to dress the site. The site is dry and not bleeding. Which dressing is recommended?
options: A sterile gauze dressing taped over the site
Gauze under a transparent film for the life of the cannula
A non-adherent pad held with a crepe bandage
A sterile transparent semipermeable dressing
B.why: NICE CG139 recommends a sterile transparent semipermeable membrane dressing, which allows the site to be observed. Gauze is for sweating or oozing sites, and is replaced as soon as possible.

whyNot.0: Gauze hides the site and is used only for sweating, bleeding or oozing.
whyNot.1: Gauze under film is a temporary option for oozing sites and should be replaced as soon as possible.
whyNot.2: A bandage obscures the site and is not the recommended dressing.

B.q: Irene, 84, has an indwelling catheter, new confusion and a temperature of 38.4°C. A catheter specimen of urine is requested. How should it be obtained?
options: Disconnect the bag and collect from the open catheter end
Pour a sample from the drainage bag outlet
Aspirate from the sampling port using aseptic technique
Remove the catheter and send the tip to the laboratory
B.why: Urine samples must be obtained from the sampling port using an aseptic technique, keeping the closed system intact (CG139 1.2.5.5).

whyNot.0: Breaking the closed system without good clinical reason increases infection risk.
whyNot.1: Urine in the bag has stood for hours and gives an unreliable result.
whyNot.3: Removing the catheter to obtain a sample is not the recommended method.

C.q: Kathleen, 90, lives at home with a long-term catheter. Her daughter asks the community nurse to start weekly bladder washouts to prevent infection. What is the best response?
options: Agree and teach the daughter to do the washouts
Explain washouts do not prevent infection; support meatal hygiene
Arrange antibiotic prophylaxis to cover each catheter change instead
Change the catheter weekly to reduce infection
C.why: CG139 states bladder instillations or washouts must not be used to prevent catheter-associated infection; daily washing of the meatus with soap and water is advised, with an individual care regimen.

whyNot.0: Washouts to prevent infection are specifically advised against and add risk by breaking the system.
whyNot.2: Prophylaxis is not offered routinely at catheter changes; it is considered after previous symptomatic UTI or trauma.
whyNot.3: Catheters are changed when clinically necessary or per manufacturer, not weekly to prevent infection.

C.q: Rajesh, 52, is on day 3 of IV antibiotics via a forearm cannula. He reports pain at the site and you see redness and swelling tracking up the vein. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Flush the cannula with 0.9% sodium chloride and recheck it in 4 hours
Apply a warm compress and continue to use the cannula
Change the dressing and clean the site with chlorhexidine
Remove the cannula and arrange resiting at a different site
C.why: Pain, redness and swelling along the vein indicate phlebitis and possible infection; the device should be removed and, if still needed, resited elsewhere. The site should be documented and monitored.

whyNot.0: Continuing to use an inflamed cannula risks worsening phlebitis and bloodstream infection.
whyNot.1: A compress does not remove the source of inflammation; the cannula should come out.
whyNot.2: A new dressing does not treat phlebitis; the device itself is the problem.

C.q: A nurse is about to give an IV bolus through a needle-free connector on Mr Obi's PICC. Which sequence follows NICE CG139 and ANTT?
options: Clean the connector, let it dry, flush, give the drug, flush, clean again
Give the drug, flush with water for injections, then clean the connector
Flush, give the drug, clean the connector with an alcohol wipe and leave wet
Clean the connector with saline, give the drug, flush with heparin each time
C.why: Hubs and ports are decontaminated with chlorhexidine in 70% alcohol before and after access and allowed to dry; lumens are flushed with sterile 0.9% sodium chloride (CG139 1.4.4).

whyNot.1: Cleaning only afterwards leaves the port contaminated at access, and 0.9% sodium chloride is the preferred flush.
whyNot.2: The connector must be cleaned before access, and antiseptic needs to dry to work.
whyNot.3: Saline does not decontaminate the port; heparin locks are used where the manufacturer recommends.

reteach.title: A chain of clean links
reteach.question: Picture the path from the syringe into the vein: which links must stay clean?

blocks.h: Find the Key-Parts, then keep them untouched
blocks.body: Imagine a chain from the drug to the bloodstream: syringe tip, port, cannula, vein. Each link that touches the next is a Key-Part, and the entry point into the body is a Key-Site. Your job is to keep those links untouched by fingers, surfaces and air for as long as possible: caps on, ports cleaned and dried, and no touching. That is all ANTT asks.

blocks.text: Asepsis depends on not touching Key-Parts and Key-Sites. Sterile gloves are needed when you must touch them, not as a substitute for non-touch technique.

explain.body: Key-Parts: critical equipment parts that contact the patient's Key-Sites, the infusion or other Key-Parts. Key-Sites: open wounds and insertion or puncture sites.

test.q: Which of these is a Key-Site?
options: The cannula insertion site
The infusion pump keypad
The tip of the giving set
The outside of the dressing pack
test.why: Key-Sites are open wounds and insertion or puncture sites for invasive devices.

whyNot.1: A pump keypad is part of the environment, not a Key-Site.
whyNot.2: The giving set tip is a Key-Part (equipment), not a Key-Site.
whyNot.3: The outside of a pack is not aseptic and is neither a Key-Part nor a Key-Site.

explain.body: Standard-ANTT: short, technically simple, few small Key-Parts, general aseptic field, usually non-sterile gloves. Surgical-ANTT: complex or prolonged, critical aseptic field such as a sterile drape, sterile gloves.

items.label: rough cut-off between Standard and Surgical

test.q: Which procedure would usually need Surgical-ANTT with a critical aseptic field?
options: Giving an IV bolus via a cannula
Inserting a urinary catheter
Changing an IV fluid bag
Taking a capillary blood sample
test.why: Urinary catheter insertion is an aseptic procedure on a sterile site needing sterile gloves and a sterile field.

whyNot.0: An IV bolus is a short, simple procedure usually done with Standard-ANTT.
whyNot.2: Changing a fluid bag protects a few small Key-Parts with Standard-ANTT.
whyNot.3: A capillary sample is a simple procedure, not needing a critical aseptic field.

explain.body: Chlorhexidine in 70% alcohol before insertion; sterile transparent dressing left in place for the life of a peripheral cannula if intact; ports cleaned before and after access; flush with sterile 0.9% sodium chloride.

test.q: How long should the transparent dressing on a peripheral cannula stay in place?
options: 24 hours, then replaced every day after that
72 hours, then replaced
For the life of the cannula, if intact
7 days, then replaced
test.why: CG139 advises leaving the transparent dressing on a peripheral cannula in place for the life of the cannula if its integrity is retained.

whyNot.0: Daily changes disturb the site without benefit.
whyNot.1: 72 hours is not the dressing interval in CG139.
whyNot.3: 7 days is the interval for central venous access device dressings.

explain.body: Aseptic insertion, closed drainage, hands and new non-sterile gloves before handling, bag below bladder and off the floor, link bag overnight, sample from the port, meatus washed daily, review and remove as soon as possible.

test.q: What volume of sterile water does NICE CG139 advise for inflating an adult catheter balloon?
options: 3 to 5 mL
30 mL
20 mL
10 mL
test.why: CG139 1.2.3.5: in general, the balloon is inflated with 10 mL of sterile water in adults and 3-5 mL in children.

whyNot.0: 3-5 mL is the guide for children.
whyNot.1: 30 mL is well above the recommended volume.
whyNot.2: 20 mL exceeds the general adult guide.
